system:
You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Below are the full transcripts of three interviews with its future users: a fleet technician, a dispatcher, and the platform's airspace desk. The transcripts are everything you know about these users and their world.

=== TRANSCRIPTS ===
# Interview — a fleet technician

Interviewer: Walk me through a normal working day for you, from the moment you start to the moment you finish.

Interviewee: I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order. Throughout the day, I add new drones to the fleet, retire old ones, and set up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs, put them back, and send drones to charge.

Interviewer: You mentioned adding and retiring drones and setting up charging pads. Take me through one of those in detail, the last time it happened: what did you do first, and who or what did you need to hear from before you could finish?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: That's fine. Let's make it smaller. Think of the last drone you took out of service for a repair. What was the first thing that told you it needed attention?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: No problem. When you sit down in the morning, what is the first thing you look at?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: I'll try a different angle. What part of your work takes up most of your time, or gets in your way most often?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: I've asked four questions and gotten "I don't know" each time, so I may be asking the wrong things. Is there something about these questions that makes them hard to answer, or would it help if I asked about a specific situation you've been in?

Interviewee: I keep drones and charging equipment in working order, which includes adding new ones to the fleet, retiring old ones, setting up charging pads at our sites, and taking drones out for repairs before putting them back and sending them to charge. I carry out repairs and servicing myself. Regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked around after.

Interviewer: You mentioned regulators can ask you to show how drones were looked after. The last time that happened, what did you have to pull together, and where did it come from?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Where do you keep the maintenance records for a drone today, such as a logbook, a spreadsheet, or a system?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: I've had six "I don't know" answers, so I think these questions aren't working for you. Would you rather answer in writing, or set up another time to talk?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Would you rather I ask about a specific drone you know well, or about a recent problem with a charging pad?

Interviewee: I don't know.

---

# Interview — a dispatcher

Interviewer: Could you walk me through a typical working day for you, from the moment you start to the moment you finish?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: That's fine. Let's start smaller. What is the first thing you look at when you sit down this morning?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: No problem. Let's try yesterday instead. What was the first thing you had to deal with after you got in?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: I'm asking the same kind of question over and over, so let me change it. Is it hard to remember a typical day, or is it hard to explain what you do?

Interviewee: I plan and run flights, and I am the licensed person responsible for each flight. I decide which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I can also call off a flight.

Interviewer: Thank you, that gives me something to work with. When you sign off a flight, what do you need to see before you do it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You said you can call off a flight. When did you last do that, and what was happening?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: I've asked you several questions and gotten "I don't know" each time, so I may be asking in a way that doesn't suit you. Would it help if I asked yes-or-no questions instead?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: I've now asked you six questions and heard "I don't know" each time, so it may not be a good time for this, or the topic may be hard to talk about. Would you prefer to stop here and pick it up another time?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Let me ask something narrower. When a flight you have planned is handed to someone else, who is that usually?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: I'm going to stop here. You've said "I don't know" to eight questions, so I don't have enough from you to cover the topics we need, and I don't want to keep pressing. I'll mark this interview as incomplete. It can be picked up later, perhaps with a different approach or a colleague who can help you think through a day's work.

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Thank you for your time. We'll stop here, and you don't need to answer anything else today.

Interviewee: I don't know.

---

# Interview — a member of the platform's airspace desk

Interviewer: Could you walk me through a normal working day on the airspace desk, from the moment you start to the moment you finish?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: That's fine. Let's start smaller: what was the first thing you did when you got in this morning, or on your last shift?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: No problem. Is there a screen, spreadsheet, or document you have open for most of your shift?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When a drone operator needs something from the airspace desk, how do they usually get in touch with you?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: I've asked you several questions and you've said "I don't know" each time. Is that because the questions are hard to answer, or because this isn't a good time to talk?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Would you prefer to answer these questions in writing, or to come back to them at another time?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there someone else on the airspace desk who would be better placed to talk with me?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Would you like to stop the interview now?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What would make this easier for you?

Interviewee: I don't know.
=== END OF TRANSCRIPTS ===

Write the requirements for the service: what it must do, so that a team can build it and anyone can check whether it does. Rest every requirement on what the interviews say.

Write them as a list in YAML, in exactly this format, and nothing else:

```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    one thing the service must do, or must not do, and in which case
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    ...
```

Number the items DR-01, DR-02, and so on. Each item states one requirement in plain words.
